title: Where Each U.S. State Gets Its Tax Revenue From
excerpt: California taxes income, while Florida and Texas rely on property tax. Each U.S. state has its own approach to raising government revenue.
content_html:
How the 50 States Generate Their Tax Revenue

Key Takeaways

  • Property taxes are the largest individual tax category in 25 states, including Florida, Texas, and New York.
  • Washington collects nearly half of its combined state and local tax revenue from general sales and gross receipts taxes.
  • Delaware stands out for license taxes, reflecting its role as a legal home for businesses.

From paychecks and purchases to homes and businesses, states rely on different combinations of taxes to fund public services.

This graphic breaks down combined state and local tax revenue across all 50 states using 2024 government finance data from the U.S. Census Bureau. The percentages show each category’s share of tax collections, excluding federal taxes and funding such as federal grants.

Property Taxes Lead in Half the Country

Property taxes are the largest revenue source in half of U.S. states, with particularly high shares in New Hampshire (64.3%), Alaska (42.4%), and Texas (41.1%). General sales and gross receipts taxes lead in 16 states, while individual income taxes top the list in seven.

The country’s largest states illustrate these differences. Individual income taxes dominate in California, while property taxes narrowly exceed general sales taxes in Florida and individual income taxes in New York.

Including local governments makes a substantial difference. In Texas, for example, property taxes are collected by local tax authorities and support services such as schools, roads, and fire protection, even though the state government itself levies no property tax.

These shares describe how governments raise money, rather than how much an individual household owes. A large property-tax share can reflect limited collections from other taxes as well as substantial property-tax revenue.

How States Fund Services Without Taxing Wages

Florida collects no individual income tax revenue, with property and general sales taxes together supplying about three-quarters of state and local tax collections. In Texas, those two categories account for nearly 79%, highlighting both states’ reliance on property and consumption taxes.

New Hampshire takes that pattern further: property taxes generated 64.3% of tax revenue, the highest share nationwide. The state has no general sales tax and does not tax wages. Its small individual income tax share in 2024 reflects the interest and dividends tax, which was repealed effective in 2025.

Sales-related collections also extend beyond the checkout counter. General sales taxes include taxes on business gross receipts, while selective sales taxes apply to particular products or activities, such as fuel, tobacco, and utilities. This helps explain why a state’s revenue mix can look different from the taxes shoppers encounter directly.

Delaware and North Dakota: The Outliers

Delaware’s largest revenue source is license taxes, accounting for roughly one-third of collections. This category includes corporate franchise licenses and related charges, giving it a much broader meaning than driver’s licenses or hunting permits.

That revenue source connects to Delaware’s position in corporate America. In 2024, the state was the legal home of more than two million business entities and about two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies. Incorporation generates public revenue from businesses whose operations extend far beyond Delaware’s borders.

North Dakota’s unusual mix reflects another economic advantage: natural resources. “Other taxes,” which include severance taxes on resource extraction, supplied 40.7% of collections. The state levies taxes on oil and gas production and oil extraction, linking part of its public finances to the value of energy produced within its borders.

Where Does Your Salary Go the Furthest in 2026?

Key Takeaways

  • Kuwait ranks first in 2026, where average salaries buy the most goods and services at local prices.
  • The U.S. ranks sixth, with salaries offering 26% more purchasing power than in Canada.
  • Cuba ranks last, followed by Syria and Nigeria, where wages buy the least at local prices.

A higher salary doesn’t always mean greater purchasing power. As housing, food, and other everyday expenses put pressure on household budgets, what matters is how much a paycheck can actually buy.

This visualization uses data from Numbeo to compare salary purchasing power across 142 countries in 2026. The index measures average take-home salaries relative to local prices, using New York City as a benchmark of 100.

Four of the five countries where salaries stretch furthest have populations below 10 million. Kuwait and Qatar lead the rankings, while Switzerland and Luxembourg also place in the top five. Oman rounds out the top five, ahead of the U.S., the world’s largest economy.

At the opposite extreme, Cuba has a purchasing power index of just 2.4, roughly 73 times lower than Kuwait’s. This highlights the enormous differences in what an average paycheck can buy across countries.

Why American Salaries Go Further Than Canadian Salaries

The purchasing power gap between the U.S. and Canada is particularly striking given the relatively high living costs in both countries.

The difference is reinforced by wage data. In 2025, average annual wages reached $86,977 in the U.S., compared with $67,901 in Canada, after adjusting for differences in local prices. That’s a 28% advantage for American workers.

Although these figures represent gross wages while Numbeo uses take-home pay, both comparisons point to a similar conclusion: the U.S. wage advantage persists even after accounting for differences in living costs.

Why Cuba Has the World’s Weakest Purchasing Power

In 2025, the average monthly state salary in Cuba was 6,930 Cuban pesos, equivalent to roughly $13 at the informal exchange rate reported in April 2026.

The country’s state-dominated wage system and depreciating currency have severely weakened household purchasing power. Food shortages, shrinking subsidized rations, and frequent power outages have compounded the pressure on households.

Why High Living Costs Don’t Always Mean Less Buying Power

Switzerland ranks third worldwide, despite being one of Europe’s most expensive countries. Portugal, where living costs are considerably lower, ranks 54th. Average salaries in Switzerland offer roughly 2.5 times the purchasing power of those in Portugal.

Oman offers another surprising example. Ranking fifth globally, ahead of the U.S., Denmark, and Australia, its strong salaries, absence of personal income tax, and relatively low living costs help explain why paychecks stretch further in the oil-rich economy.

These comparisons highlight why affordability depends on both earnings and expenses. Countries with high living costs can still offer strong purchasing power when local wages are high enough to offset them.

Mapped: Where Americans Have the Most Debt Per Person

Americans owe trillions in personal debt. See how much residents owe in every state, and why some carry nearly three times as much.

How Personal Debt Varies Across America

Key Takeaways

  • Americans with a credit report carry an average of $63,200 in personal debt, including mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and student loans.
  • Washington, D.C. has the highest average debt at $102,400 per person, nearly three times West Virginia’s $37,900.
  • Colorado ranks second nationally at $92,690, ahead of California, Washington, and Hawaii.

Americans owe trillions of dollars across mortgages, credit cards, auto loans, and student debt. But the amount people owe varies dramatically by location, with some of the highest balances concentrated in expensive housing markets.

This graphic maps average debt per person by state using Q4 2025 data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

The figures cover residents with a credit report and combine major forms of household borrowing, making the map a measure of outstanding debt balances rather than financial distress or ability to repay.

Where Americans Carry the Most Personal Debt

Washington, D.C. leads the country in average personal debt, followed by Colorado and California. Colorado’s second-place ranking is particularly notable, putting it ahead of several states known for expensive housing, including California and Hawaii.

At the other end of the spectrum, West Virginia, Mississippi, and Arkansas have the lowest average debt balances.

Housing helps explain large differences in personal debt between states. In Colorado, mortgages account for 78% of average personal debt, compared with 55% in West Virginia.

Nationally, mortgages made up roughly 70% of America’s $18.8 trillion in household debt at the end of 2025. Because mortgages make up such a large share of debt, higher home prices can translate into larger average debt balances.

What Higher Debt Means for Americans Today

The amount Americans owe tells only part of the story. Monthly payments, interest rates, and household income ultimately determine how manageable that debt is.

For instance, Harvard’s 2026 housing report found that homeowners who moved in before 2020 had median first-mortgage payments roughly $800 lower per month than more recent movers, based on 2024 data.

For households facing higher housing costs and borrowing rates, those monthly payments can leave significantly less room for savings and everyday expenses.

The key distinction is between how much Americans owe and how difficult that debt is to repay. A homeowner with a large, low-interest mortgage may face less financial pressure than someone with a smaller balance carrying much higher interest costs.

These shares describe how governments raise money, rather than how much an individual household owes. A large property-tax share can reflect limited collections from other taxes as well as substantial property-tax revenue.

How States Fund Services Without Taxing Wages

Florida collects no individual income tax revenue, with property and general sales taxes together supplying about three-quarters of state and local tax collections. In Texas, those two categories account for nearly 79%, highlighting both states’ reliance on property and consumption taxes.

New Hampshire takes that pattern further: property taxes generated 64.3% of tax revenue, the highest share nationwide. The state has no general sales tax and does not tax wages. Its small individual income tax share in 2024 reflects the interest and dividends tax, which was repealed effective in 2025.

Sales-related collections also extend beyond the checkout counter. General sales taxes include taxes on business gross receipts, while selective sales taxes apply to particular products or activities, such as fuel, tobacco, and utilities. This helps explain why a state’s revenue mix can look different from the taxes shoppers encounter directly.

Delaware and North Dakota: The Outliers

Delaware’s largest revenue source is license taxes, accounting for roughly one-third of collections. This category includes corporate franchise licenses and related charges, giving it a much broader meaning than driver’s licenses or hunting permits.

That revenue source connects to Delaware’s position in corporate America. In 2024, the state was the legal home of more than two million business entities and about two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies. Incorporation generates public revenue from businesses whose operations extend far beyond Delaware’s borders.

North Dakota’s unusual mix reflects another economic advantage: natural resources. “Other taxes,” which include severance taxes on resource extraction, supplied 40.7% of collections. The state levies taxes on oil and gas production and oil extraction, linking part of its public finances to the value of energy produced within its borders.

Why American Salaries Go Further Than Canadian Salaries

The purchasing power gap between the U.S. and Canada is particularly striking given the relatively high living costs in both countries.

The difference is reinforced by wage data. In 2025, average annual wages reached $86,977 in the U.S., compared with $67,901 in Canada, after adjusting for differences in local prices. That’s a 28% advantage for American workers.

Although these figures represent gross wages while Numbeo uses take-home pay, both comparisons point to a similar conclusion: the U.S. wage advantage persists even after accounting for differences in living costs.

Why Cuba Has the World’s Weakest Purchasing Power

In 2025, the average monthly state salary in Cuba was 6,930 Cuban pesos, equivalent to roughly $13 at the informal exchange rate reported in April 2026.

The country’s state-dominated wage system and depreciating currency have severely weakened household purchasing power. Food shortages, shrinking subsidized rations, and frequent power outages have compounded the pressure on households.

Why High Living Costs Don’t Always Mean Less Buying Power

Switzerland ranks third worldwide, despite being one of Europe’s most expensive countries. Portugal, where living costs are considerably lower, ranks 54th. Average salaries in Switzerland offer roughly 2.5 times the purchasing power of those in Portugal.

Oman offers another surprising example. Ranking fifth globally, ahead of the U.S., Denmark, and Australia, its strong salaries, absence of personal income tax, and relatively low living costs help explain why paychecks stretch further in the oil-rich economy.

These comparisons highlight why affordability depends on both earnings and expenses. Countries with high living costs can still offer strong purchasing power when local wages are high enough to offset them.
